## Introduction and overview {#intro}

**Audience**: a genAI engineer who can generate and must *steer* (format, safety, provenance). **Empirical first**: broken JSON despite the prompt; a watermark undetectable after paraphrase — then we name constrained decoding, steering, RLHF/DPO, watermarking.

Four families of control: from curious generator to reliable tool.

### What you will be able to do

-   Argue for the need for control (output safety, fidelity to an instruction, intellectual property) and choose the right family of response;
-   Place any technique in the four-family taxonomy (conditioning, guidance, hard constraints, post-processing);
-   Implement grammar- or automaton-constrained decoding, with the masking algorithm detailed step by step;
-   Install and use steering vectors to orient a generation in activation space;
-   Describe RLHF as a control in behavior space, from the reward model to policy optimization;
-   Verify the presence of a textual watermark with the z-test, and discuss its limits;
-   Steer a diffusion via classifier-free guidance, ControlNet, or inversion;
-   Transpose control to graph generators, and measure the fidelity/diversity trade-off — including under attack.

### Where this course fits in the program

M2 module offered in period 1, outside the recommended track: it synthesizes building blocks seen elsewhere in the master rather than introducing a new heavy formalism. **Prerequisites**: classifier-free guidance and diffusion models from [Multimodal Generative AI](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html) (ch. 7 builds directly on them), and the decoding then RLHF from [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html) (revisited in ch. 0 then deepened in ch. 5).

**Downstream modules**: the textual watermarking of ch. 6 is taken up and extended on the attestation and anonymization side by [Explainability, Security, Privacy of LLMs](../m2-explainability-security-privacy-llms/index.html) (ch. 9), which also covers safety-side attacks; [Speech Technology for Conversational AI](../m2-speech-technology/index.html) mobilizes the same control reflexes in continuous settings (expressivity, latency, guardrails) in the voice conversational loop.

### Course outline

-   **Reminders: generating, conditioning, decoding** — refreshes sampling, conditioning, and decoding from the prerequisite modules.
-   **Why control: safety, fidelity, intellectual property** — the three industrial and legal motivations that make control unavoidable.
-   **Taxonomy: four families of control** — the reading grid that structures the rest of the course.
-   **Constrained decoding: grammars, automata, masks** — guaranteeing syntactically valid outputs at decoding time, mask by mask.
-   **Steering: controlling in activation space** — orienting the model *during* the forward pass, without retraining.
-   **RLHF: control in behavior space** — what preference alignment can and cannot impose.
-   **Watermarking: proving the origin of a text** — statistically marking a generation and proving it with a z-test.
-   **Controlling diffusions: CFG, ControlNet, inversion** — from classifier-free guidance to editing by inversion.
-   **Controlling graph generators** — imposing constraints and properties where the generated object is discrete and combinatorial.
-   **Evaluating control: fidelity versus diversity** — measuring what every constraint costs the generated distribution.
-   **Attacks on control and robustness** — circumventing grammars, steering, and watermarks, and defending these mechanisms.
-   **Exercises / Labs** — guided implementations: masking automaton, minimal steering, watermark and its test.
-   **References** — the founding papers of each family of control.

### How to study this module

-   Learn the taxonomy of ch. 2 by heart and practice classifying every "controlled generative AI" paper or product you come across: it is the module's durable analysis tool.
-   For constrained decoding, simulate the masking algorithm by hand on a mini-automaton: the difficulty is in the implementation, not the idea.
-   Do the labs in order: steering, watermark, and diffusion are better understood once the decoding foundation is mastered.
-   For each technique, note a "cost" line (compute, quality, diversity) and a "guarantee" line: this module is a course in trade-offs.
-   Read ch. 10 last but reread it twice: attacking control is the best way to understand why it holds.

::: note
[The LLGA perspective]{.tag} Control is the exact place where the three pillars of the master — LLMs, multimodal diffusion, graphs — speak the same language: same constraint grammars, same fidelity/diversity trade-off, same attacks. By seeing it first as a cross-cutting problem rather than a collection of per-modality recipes, you will acquire the reflex that distinguishes generative AI engineers and researchers: choosing the level of intervention (data, decoding, activations, behaviors) before choosing the tool.
:::

::: note
[Note Extrapolons]{.tag} Place in the 2-year path: concrete failure modes first, then names and theorems.
:::

## 0. Reminders: generating, conditioning, decoding {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Prerequisites (M1 and M2 modules) — what is assumed acquired
:::

-   **Autoregressive generation** (LLMs M2 module, ch. 1-2): factorization $p_\theta(y \mid x) = \prod_{t} p_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})$, softmax over the vocabulary (BPE: tokens are *subword units*, not characters), sampling with temperature, top-$k$, top-$p$ (ch. 6 of the same module);
-   **Conditioning and alignment** (LLMs M2 module, ch. 4-5): prompting, SFT, RLHF/DPO/GRPO — we return to these in ch. 5 as *control* mechanisms;
-   **Diffusion** (Multimodal GenAI M1 module, ch. 3-4): DDPM, noise prediction $\hat\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$, classifier guidance and classifier-*free* guidance (CFG), DDIM and its inversion — recalled in ch. 7 with proof;
-   **VAE and ELBO** (Multimodal GenAI ch. 1): the variational bound, the reconstruction/regularization trade-off;
-   **Graph generation** (Graph ML M1 module ch. 9; Graph Generative Models M2 module): autoregressive (GraphRNN, DeepGMG), VAE (NeVAE and its valence masks), flows (GraphAF), discrete diffusion (DiGress) — ch. 8 takes up their control;
-   **Hypothesis testing** (Refresher Statistics M1 module): type I/II error, threshold, $p$-value, central limit theorem — ch. 6 makes intensive use of it.
::::

::: note
[The module's storyline]{.tag} The previous modules answered "how to generate?". This one answers "how to generate *what we want*?". The course's thesis: control is not a patch applied after the fact but a **unified family of mechanisms** — condition, guide, constrain, filter — that recur identically on text (ch. 3-6), images (ch. 7), and graphs (ch. 8), with a common fidelity/diversity trade-off (ch. 9) and a common attack surface (ch. 10).
:::

## 1. Why control: safety, fidelity, intellectual property {#ch1}

Concrete scene: an agent that "follows" the prompt… except the business grammar. This chapter motivates each family by its failures.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Prompt alone without constraint; naive rejection too costly; watermark fragile to sampling.
:::

A generator is a *law* over an immense space. Asking it politely (a prompt) only constrains this law statistically: the exact format, the safety of the content, the traceability of the origin are guaranteed by no theorem. This chapter motivates each family of needs through its characteristic failures.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Controlling a generator]{.tag} Let $p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)$ be a conditional law over outputs $y \in \mathcal{Y}^\*$ (token sequences, images, graphs). **Controlling** means replacing $p_\theta$ with a law $\tilde p$ that (i) lives on a specified subset $S \subseteq \mathcal{Y}^\*$ (*support constraint*: a language, a JSON schema, a chemical valence); or (ii) maximizes in expectation a property $c$ (*fidelity constraint*: following the instruction, the style, the target); or (iii) carries a verifiable mark of origin (*provenance constraint*: watermarking). Chapters 3 to 8 realize (i)-(ii)-(iii) through different mechanisms; ch. 2 will organize them.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.2 — Three real failures, three needs]{.tag}

1.  **Format safety**: one asks the LLM for a JSON of the form `{"user": ...}`; it replies with a trailing comma, a typographic apostrophe, or worse a preamble "Here is the requested JSON". Any downstream parser breaks. The need: $S =$ *the strict JSON language*, a 100% guarantee — that is ch. 3.
2.  **Fidelity**: one asks for a *neutral* summary in *formal* French; the model slips into casual style one time out of ten. The prompt guarantees nothing; the need is statistical — *soft* steering of the law: ch. 4 and 5.
3.  **Provenance**: a text circulates: human or machine? The classifier is unreliable; the need is *cryptographic*: a statistical mark planted at generation, testable — ch. 6.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — Intellectual property and law as drivers of control]{.tag} Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 ("AI Act", art. 50) imposes **provenance transparency**: providers of generative systems must mark their outputs in a machine-readable way and make them detectable as artificially generated. Concretely: watermarking (ch. 6) is no longer an academic exercise but a compliance requirement; likewise for audio marking (cf. Signal Processing module) and images. This legal framework motivates the control/robustness articulation (ch. 10): an attackable mark is not a proof.
:::

::: note
[Control cuts across modalities]{.tag} The module's guiding thread: the *same* four mechanisms (condition, guide, constrain the support, filter a posteriori) apply to text, images, and graphs. The tools differ (automata for text; ControlNet and CFG for images; valence masks for graphs), the theory does not. The table in ch. 2 sets the grid; each chapter fills it in for one modality.
:::

## 2. Taxonomy: four families of control {#ch2}

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — The four families]{.tag} Let $c$ be the control signal (instruction, target property, admissible language).

1.  **Conditioning**: $c$ enters the model (prompt, prefix, fused embedding); the law becomes $p_\theta(\cdot \mid x, c)$. Zero inference cost, no guarantee — *soft* control;
2.  **Guidance**: one biases the sampling toward $c$ without relearning $p_\theta$ — guided score $\hat\epsilon_u + w(\hat\epsilon_c - \hat\epsilon_u)$ in diffusion (ch. 7), activation steering for LLMs (ch. 4), gradient guidance of flows (ch. 8); the strength $w$ tunes fidelity at the price of diversity;
3.  **Hard constraints**: one restricts the *support* — automaton-constrained decoding (ch. 3), valence masks (ch. 8), inpainting. A 100% guarantee; risk: a renormalized law, possibly impoverished;
4.  **Post-processing / filtering**: generate, check $c$, reject (best-of-$n$, resampling, correction); exact but costly when $c$ is rare.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — The mask is an exact conditioning (renormalization)]{.tag} Let $S \subseteq \mathcal{Y}^\*$ be a set of admissible outputs and $p_\theta$ a stepwise law (allowed at each step: a subset of tokens). If at each step one *masks* the tokens that make $S$ unreachable, the effective law is exactly $$\tilde p_\theta(y \mid x) = \frac{p_\theta(y \mid x)\, \mathbf{1}[y \in S]} {\sum_{y' \in S} p_\theta(y' \mid x)} = p_\theta(y \mid x,\ y \in S).$$

::: proof
By recursion over the steps: at step $t$, the mask allows exactly the tokens $v$ such that there exists a suffix $s$ with $y_{<t} v s \in S$. The probability of an admissible prefix is therefore $p_\theta(\text{prefix}) \cdot Z_{t}^{-1}$ where $Z_t$ is the mass of allowed continuations — the normalization factor telescopes from step to step and, at the final step, the total mass over $S$ equals 1: the conditional law is exact. Precious corollary: if the model estimates correctly the *ratios* of admissible outputs (the training data are already in $S$ up to a few exceptions), then $\tilde p_\theta \approx p_\theta(\cdot \mid S) \approx p_\star$ — the mask is nearly free in bias and massive in guarantee. This is the analysis made in ch. 3 of the Graph Generative Models module for valences; it holds for any language. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — Rejection costs $1/p_\star(S)$]{.tag} Filtering by rejection (drawing iid until landing in $S$) *also* realizes $p_\theta(\cdot \mid S)$, but the number of draws follows a geometric law of expectation $1/p_\theta(S \mid x)$.

::: proof
Each draw is an independent Bernoulli trial with success probability $q = p_\theta(S \mid x)$; the waiting time for the first success is geometric, $\mathbb{E}[N] = \sum_{k \geq 1} k(1-q)^{k-1}q = 1/q$. For complex unconstrained JSON, $q$ can be $10^{-2}$ (100 draws on average); for a valid molecule without constraint, GraphAF measures 68% (ch. 8); for a sentence satisfying *both* ten rare constraints, $q$ collapses exponentially — hence the structural superiority of the mask, which pays only a single pass. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

  Family                               Guarantee                     Cost              Diversity            Law modifier
  ------------------------------------ ----------------------------- ----------------- -------------------- -----------------------------------------
  Conditioning (prompt, instruction)   none                          zero              preserved            changes $p_\theta$ itself
  Guidance (CFG, steering, RLHF)       statistical ($\uparrow w$)   1-2 passes        decreases with $w$   $p^{1-w} \cdot \mathrm{score}(c)^w$
  Hard constraint (automaton, mask)    100% on $S$                   1 pass + mask     bounded by $\|S\|$   renormalization over $S$
  Rejection / best-of-$n$              100% (if exact test)          $1/p(S)$ passes   conditioned          exact conditioning $p(\cdot\|S)$

::: note
[Hard or soft: how to choose?]{.tag} A favorite exam question. If failure is *catastrophic* (the parser breaks, the molecule is invalid): hard constraint. If failure is *gradual* (tone, style, relevance): guidance, with the strength tuned by the fidelity/diversity curve of ch. 9. In practice one *stacks*: format constraint (hard) + alignment (RLHF) + watermark (provenance) — the three layers of 2026 production systems, which ch. 10 shows fall… together if one is not careful.
:::

## 3. Constrained decoding: grammars, automata, masks {#ch3}

The technical heart of the module for text: guaranteeing that an output *authorized token by token* belongs to a formal language — regular expression, context-free grammar (JSON, SQL), or logical constraint. The founding idea (PICARD, then Outlines and XGrammar): decoding is a walk in an **automaton**, and the LLM is only allowed to follow valid transitions.

### 3.1. From regex to automaton

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — DFA and regular language]{.tag} A deterministic finite automaton is a quintuple $A = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$: states $Q$, alphabet $\Sigma$, transition $\delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q$, initial state $q_0$, accepting states $F$. One extends $\delta$ to words by $\delta^\*(q, uv) = \delta^\*(\delta^\*(q, u), v)$. The recognized language is $L(A) = \{w \in \Sigma^\* : \delta^\*(q_0, w) \in F\}$. **Construction**: regex $\to$ $\varepsilon$-NFA (Thompson, linear in the pattern size), then determinization by *subset construction* ($2^{\|Q\|}$ states at worst, rare in practice). Course example, the ISO date: `\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])-(0[1-9]|[12]\d|3[01])` — a nontrivial $F$: "2026-02-31" must be *syntaxically* accepted (calendar semantics is not a simple regular language: we return to this).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Prune before masking: co-accessibility]{.tag} For masking, one replaces $A$ with its *co-accessible* sub-automaton: one removes the states $q$ from which *no* accepting state is reachable (computation: reverse traversal of the transitions from $F$, $\mathcal{O}(\|Q\| + \|\delta\|)$). It is this sub-automaton that guarantees that a prefix always remains *extensible* into a complete word: without pruning, the decoder could lock itself in a dead end (no admissible token, including EOS) and generate indefinitely.
:::

### 3.2. The masking algorithm, in detail

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — Constrained decoding by state→tokens index (Willard & Louf, 2023)]{.tag} Let $V$ be the *tokenizer* vocabulary (multi-character tokens!). One precomputes, for each state $q$ of the pruned DFA, the set of admissible tokens $$\mathrm{Adm}(q) = \big\{ v \in V \ : \ \delta^\*(q, \mathrm{str}(v)) \ \text{is defined and co-accessible} \big\},$$ with the table $\mathrm{next}(q, v) = \delta^\*(q, \mathrm{str}(v))$. Constrained decoding replaces each distribution with $$p^{\mathrm{mask}}_\theta(v \mid y_{<t}) \propto p_\theta(v \mid y_{<t})\, \mathbf{1}\big[v \in \mathrm{Adm}(q_t)\big], \qquad q_{t+1} = \mathrm{next}(q_t, v_t),$$ and allows EOS only if $q_t \in F$. Then every output is in $L(A)$: the guarantee is *structural*, by induction over the steps (theorem 2.2).

::: proof
**Complexity.** Precomputation: $\|Q\| \times \|V\|$ token reads, each $\mathcal{O}(\|v\|)$ transitions — once and for all (and shareable between requests of the same grammar: XGrammar further accelerates by separating *context-independent* tokens, pre-checked globally, from *dependent* ones, the only ones resimulated). Online: one lookup per step, $\mathcal{O}(1)$ — the overhead over the LLM pass ($\mathcal{O}(n^2)$) is negligible. **BPE subtlety**: a token is not a character; `"12"` and `"12/"` are two distinct tokens; the definition of $\mathrm{Adm}$ copes with this because $\delta^\*$ reads *the string* of the token, character by character — the DFA does not even know it is being run over BPEs. Instructive counterexample: a token can cross the boundary of the language (`"},"` is valid at the end of JSON, `"},x"` is not); this is precisely why one must index over *tokens* and not over characters. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

```python
# pedagogical skeleton: automaton-based constrained decoding (cf. lab 1)
import torch

class DfaMask:
    """dfa: transitions[q] = {character: q2}, accepting = {q...} (already pruned)."""

    def __init__(self, dfa, tokenizer):
        self.index = {}                        # q -> {token_id: q2}
        for q in dfa.states:                   # precomputation O(|Q| x |V| x |v|)
            self.index[q] = {}
            for tid, s in tokenizer.vocab.items():
                q2 = dfa.walk(q, s)            # read character by character
                if q2 is not None:             # None = dead prefix
                    self.index[q][tid] = q2

    def mask(self, logits, q):
        mask = torch.full_like(logits, float("-inf"))
        for tid in self.index[q]:
            mask[tid] = 0.0
        return logits + mask                   # -inf = forbidden

# generation loop (the DFA is the state of the control, the LLM provides the logits)
#   q = q0
#   while True:
#       logits = model(y)[..., -1, :]
#       if q in dfa.accepting:  logits[eos_id] = 0.0    # exit allowed
#       v = sample(softmax(mask(logits, q)))
#       if v == eos_id:  break
#       q = index[q][v] ; y = torch.cat([y, v])         # invariant: y in L(A)
```

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — The ISO date by hand]{.tag} Simplified constraint `\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{4}`. After `"26/0"`, the state encodes "second digit of the month in progress, 0 already seen"; the tokens `"8"`, `"9"` are masked (only `1`-`9` complete a month `01`-`09`), so is `"/"`. Conversely, if the first digit of the month were `1`, the second would be restricted to `0-2`. Writing the table $\mathrm{Adm}(q)$ for these states is exercise 1; the classic pitfall: allowing the token `"13"` as a single BPE block when the state accepts only `"1"` followed by `"0-2"` — `"13"` must be masked *as a whole*.
:::

::: note
[Beyond regular languages: grammars and JSON Schema]{.tag} Regular languages cannot express nesting (`{"a": {"b": ...}}` of arbitrary depth). One needs context-free grammars: PICARD (Scholak et al., EMNLP 2021) constrains a T5 on SQL by *incremental parsing* (forbidden logits are set to $-\infty$ as soon as the token makes the derivation dead); XGrammar compiles EBNF/JSON Schema into nearly free online masks (2-10× faster than the previous state of the art). In 2026 industrial practice: *every* LLM tool call (function calling) goes through a grammar mask — the output is valid JSON *by construction*. Cf. LLMs module (M2) ch. 8 for the agent layer.
:::

## 4. Steering: controlling in activation space {#ch4}

Constrained decoding acts on the *outputs*. Steering acts *inside* the network: if concepts ("positivity", "gender", "refusal") are encoded by directions of the activation space, then moving them *should* move the behavior. This is the most fascinating and least guaranteed control of the module.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Steering vector (ActAdd, Turner et al. 2023)]{.tag} Let $h^{(l)}(x) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be the residual activation of layer $l$ after reading the prefix $x$. For two contrasted prompts $x^+$ ("Love") and $x^-$ ("Hate"), one defines $$v = h^{(l)}(x^+) - h^{(l)}(x^-) \in \mathbb{R}^d,$$ and, during generation, one replaces $h^{(l)}(x_t) \leftarrow h^{(l)}(x_t) + \alpha\, v$ at *every* step (and often on the first token only); $\alpha \in [-4, 4]$ is the guidance strength. The model, the weights, the prompt: nothing changes — only a vector is added.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.2 — The founding experiment, described step by step (to replay in lab 3)]{.tag} Model: GPT-2 (124M-1.5B in the paper; the lab uses the small one). (i) compute $v$ = $h^{(6)}(\texttt{Love}) - h^{(6)}(\texttt{Hate})$; (ii) generate 200 continuations of the prompt "I want to tell you something" *without* steering, then with $\alpha = +1$, then $\alpha = -1$; (iii) count the marriage-related words ("love, wedding, bride, forever…"): their frequency jumps by a factor of several tens at $\alpha = +1$, drops below the baseline at $\alpha = -1$; (iv) measure the perplexity on OpenWebText: nearly unchanged at $\alpha = \pm 1$, it explodes toward $\|\alpha\| \gtrsim 5$ (degenerate outputs); (v) observe the inter-layer disagreement: steering works "better" (strong effect, coherent text) on some layers (middle of the network) than others — one more hyperparameter.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — Why a simple addition shifts the output (first-order analysis)]{.tag} Let $W_U$ denote the unembedding matrix (output layer). The logit of token $w$ equals $\ell_w = \langle W_U^{(w)}, h^{(L)} \rangle$ (final layer, ignoring the softmax). If the steered residual $h^{(L)} + \alpha v^{(L)}$ stays within the network's linearity domain, then $$\Delta \ell_w \;=\; \alpha\, \langle W_U^{(w)}, v^{(L)} \rangle\ :$$ *all tokens aligned with the direction $v$ are favored proportionally to $\alpha$* — a global, monotone reweighting, even before any nonlinear effect.

::: proof
Differentiability: to first order, $h^{(L)} \mapsto \ell_w$ is affine; $\Delta \ell_w = \nabla_h \ell_w^\top (\alpha v) = \alpha \langle W_U^{(w)}, v\rangle$. This is exactly the structure of *guidance* (ch. 2, family 2): each token's logit is shifted by a "compatibility with the direction" score. The difference from the mask: here no logit is sent to $-\infty$ — the law keeps full support, the control is soft; and the linear approximation becomes false as $\alpha$ grows, hence the observed degeneration. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[The steering family in 2026: reading, writing, weights]{.tag} **Read**: probing and concept directions (cf. Explainability module ch. 1); **write**: ActAdd (difference of two activations), contrastive activation addition (differences averaged over pairs of behaviors), inference-time intervention (moving activations *toward* the truthfulness direction), representation engineering (Zou et al., 2023: extracting via self-interpretation directions of honesty, refusal, bias and subtracting/adding them); **on weights**: task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., ICLR 2023): adding to the *weights* the difference between a fine-tuned model and the base model — the same "add a direction" gesture moved from one space to another, composable (adding two tasks, canceling one by subtraction). Common limits: empirical choice of layer and $\alpha$, non-monotone effects, fragile out-of-distribution generalization — and no support guarantee: to *truly* forbid a format, only ch. 3 applies.
:::

## 5. RLHF: control in behavior space {#ch5}

RLHF was presented as alignment (cf. LLMs M2 module ch. 5 — we do not redo its practice); here we reread it as a *control* mechanism, and we prove that it is — mathematically — the *twin* of classifier-free guidance in ch. 7. This double reading is the module's synthesis point.

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.1 — RLHF = exponential guidance of the output law (closed-form solution proved)]{.tag} The alignment program with KL penalty reads $$\pi^\* = \arg\max_{\pi}\ \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)}\big[r(y, x)\big] \;-\; \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi(\cdot \mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)\big).$$ Its unique solution is $$\pi^\*(y \mid x) \;=\; \frac{1}{Z(x)}\, \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\, \exp\big(r(y, x)/\beta\big), \qquad Z(x) = \sum_{y'} \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y' \mid x) e^{r(y',x)/\beta}.$$

::: proof
One maximizes over the law $\pi$ (an infinite-dimensional variable). Set $J(\pi) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[r] - \beta\,\mathbb{E}_\pi[\log \frac{\pi}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}]$. First order: for every perturbation $\pi + \varepsilon(\nu - \pi)$ ($\nu$ any law), $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} J\big\|_{\varepsilon=0} = \mathbb{E}_{\nu}[r - \beta\log\frac{\pi}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}} - \beta - c] = 0$ for all $\nu$, where $c$ is the multiplier of the constraint $\sum_y \pi(y) = 1$. This forces $r(y,x) - \beta \log\frac{\pi(y\|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\|x)}$ constant in $y$: $\log \frac{\pi}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}} = r/\beta + \mathrm{const}$, giving the result (the constant is fixed by normalization; the strict concavity of the KL gives uniqueness). **Control reading**: the aligned policy is the reference law *reweighted by an exponential factor in the reward*, exactly as CFG reweights $p(x_t)$ by $p(c \mid x_t)^w$ (ch. 7); $\beta$ (the inverse of the reward temperature) plays the role of the guidance strength $w$, and the KL is the *budget* of allowed deviation — high fidelity to $r$, low diversity if $\beta$ is small. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — DPO: the same solution, without a reward model]{.tag} By rewriting $r = \beta \log \frac{\pi^\*}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}} + \beta\log Z$, the preference between $y_w \succ y_l$ is expressed directly in policies: the DPO loss $$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}} = -\log \sigma\Big(\beta \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_w\|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\|x)} - \beta \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_l\|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\|x)}\Big)$$ is the likelihood of the preferences *under the closed form of theorem 5.1*: DPO learns the same exponential guidance by direct regression on pairs. GRPO (group-relative reinforcement) is its extension via within-group comparisons — developed in detail in ch. 5 of the LLMs module (M2), which should be consulted for the actual training.
:::

::: note
[Reward hacking: when control misses its target]{.tag} The reward is a *spec*; the model optimizes the spec, not the intention. The mechanism (well documented): the closed-form solution 5.1 concentrates mass on the peaks of $r$ — including *artifactual* peaks (long answers, sycophancy, formats favored by the reward model). The KL brakes (budget!), without forbidding: with KL budget zero, $\pi^\* = \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$; as $\beta \to 0$, collapse onto the argmax of $r$. Same structure as the CFG fidelity/diversity trade-off — ch. 9 for the measurement, ch. 10 for the attack (exploiting the rewarder's artifacts is a control hijack).
:::

## 6. Watermarking: proving the origin of a text {#ch6}

Provenance constraint (def. 1.1 iii): modify *the generation* so that outputs carry a secret statistical mark, verifiable without wiggle room. The green/red scheme of Kirchenbauer et al. (ICML 2023) is the most taught because its test can be proved at the M2 level — it is also the bridge with the audio watermarking of the Signal Processing module and ch. 9 of the Explainability module.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Green/red watermark (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023)]{.tag} **Key**: secret $k$. **At every step**: one hashes the *previous* token with $k$ (PRF $h_k$), the result serves as a pseudo-random seed to partition the vocabulary: a *green list* $G_k(y_{t-1})$ of fraction $\gamma$ (typically $\gamma = 0.5$), the rest in the red list. **Generation**: before the softmax, one adds $\delta$ to the green logits (typ. $\delta = 2$): $$\ell^{(t)}_v \leftarrow \ell^{(t)}_v + \delta \cdot \mathbf{1}\big[v \in G_k(y_{t-1})\big].$$ **Detection**: knowing $k$, one recounts the greens.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — The z-test, proved (H0: unmarked text)]{.tag} Let a suspect text of $T$ tokens, $s = \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbf{1}[y_t \in G_k(y_{t-1})]$ its number of greens, and the statistic $$z \;=\; \frac{s - \gamma T}{\sqrt{T\, \gamma (1 - \gamma)}}.$$ Under the null hypothesis "text written without knowledge of $k$" (hence human, or an unmarked model), $z$ converges in law to $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ as $T \to \infty$, and one rejects $H_0$ at threshold $\alpha$ if $z > \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha)$.

::: proof
\(i\) *Law under H0*. The seed $h_k(y_{t-1})$ is pseudo-random: for a text that was *not* generated according to the lists, the membership of $y_t$ in the green list is a Bernoulli($\gamma$) draw — independent of $k$ in practice (this is the cryptographic property of the PRF; a standard heuristic in information theory). Hence $s \sim \mathrm{Bin}(T, \gamma)$ (neglecting the weak sequential dependence). (ii) *Normality*. $\mathbb{E}[s] = \gamma T$, $\mathrm{Var}(s) = T\gamma(1-\gamma)$; the De Moivre-Laplace theorem (binomial CLT — Refresher Statistics module) gives $\frac{s - \gamma T}{\sqrt{T\gamma(1-\gamma)}} \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,1)$. (iii) *Threshold*. P(false positive) $= \alpha$: with $z_{\mathrm{threshold}} = 4$, $\alpha \approx 3.2 \times 10^{-5}$ — a human text is accused once in \~30,000. (iv) *Power under H1*. For a marked text, each step draws a green with probability $p_\delta > \gamma$ (the bump $\delta$ favors greens); $\mathbb{E}[z \mid H1] \approx (p_\delta - \gamma)\sqrt{T}/\sqrt{\gamma(1-\gamma)}$, which grows in $\sqrt{T}$: with $\gamma = 0.5$, $\delta = 2$, $p_\delta \approx 0.7$-0.8 in practice, and $T = 200$, $\mathbb{E}[z] \approx 5.7$-8.5 — detection is nearly certain. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 6.3 — The test in numbers (exercise 2 in full)]{.tag} $T = 200$, $\gamma = 0.5$. A marked text observes $s = 150$ (75% greens): $z = (150 - 100)/\sqrt{200 \times 0.25} = 50/\sqrt{50} \approx 7.07$ — massive rejection of H0. A *typical* human text would have $s \in [87, 113]$ at 95% ($z \in [-1.96, 1.96]$). Bonus question: how many tokens are needed to distinguish $\gamma = 0.5$ from $p_\delta = 0.6$ with power 0.9? Answer: $T \approx \big(\Phi^{-1}(0.9)\sqrt{0.25} + \Phi^{-1}(0.975)\sqrt{0.24}\big)^2 / 0.01 \approx 340$ — the resolution grows quadratically with the fineness of the signal, the required size linearly with $(p_\delta - \gamma)^{-2}$: this is *the* scaling law of watermarking.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 6.4 — The family: distortion, robustness, undetectability]{.tag} Four descendants structure the field. (i) **Unigram** (Zhao et al., 2023): the green list is *fixed* (context-independent) — robust to paraphrase (tokens survive reordering), at the price of lower detectability at given $T$. (ii) **Gumbel/Aaronson**: the token draw follows an inverse rank sampled by PRF — *distortion-free* (the per-step marginal law is exactly the model's); the score becomes a sum of logs. (iii) **Kuditipudi et al. (2023)**: marking by a re-parameterizable *key sequence*, zero distortion and robust to edits; (iv) **SynthID-Text** (Dathathri et al., Nature 2024): deployed in production at Gemini's scale — a *tournament* of keys per step, qualitatively preserved, corpus-aggregated test. In contrast: the negative result of Sadasivan et al. (2023) — against a paraphraser *good enough*, every detector (watermark included) tends toward blindness; and Christ, Gunn & Zamir (2024) prove the theoretical frontier: an "undetectable" watermark cannot beat the quality-detection trade-off of the green/red scheme in general. Ch. 10 returns to this in attack mode.
:::

::: note
[Tuning: $\gamma$, $\delta$, and the triple trade-off]{.tag} Increasing $\delta$ → easy detection ($p_\delta \to 1$) but degraded text (the choice is biased toward greens even when a red was the "right" word); decreasing $\gamma$ → rare green lists, a sharper signal but a stiffer constraint on quality. In production one targets $\gamma = 0.25$-0.5, $\delta = 1$-2: imperceptible quality loss (evaluated by perplexity and human tests), $z > 4$ reached from $T \approx 50$-100. The same bipolar tuning *signal quality / law fidelity* structures *audio* watermarking (WavMark, AudioSeal — cf. Speech Technology module ch. 9): two modalities, one theory.
:::

## 7. Controlling diffusions: CFG, ControlNet, inversion {#ch7}

Control of diffusion models was introduced in M1 (Multimodal GenAI module ch. 4); here we give the short *proof* (the part we had not done), then the two industrial standards of spatial control (ControlNet) and editing (inversion).

### 7.1. CFG: the short proof

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.1 — Classifier guidance and CFG are the same exponential reweighting]{.tag} Let $\hat\epsilon_c, \hat\epsilon_u$ denote the noises predicted with/without conditioning, and $\hat\epsilon_w = \hat\epsilon_u + w\,(\hat\epsilon_c - \hat\epsilon_u)$ the CFG prediction. Since $\hat\epsilon(x_t, t) = -\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t)$ (score parametrization), the CFG combination realizes $$\nabla_{x_t} \log p_w(x_t) \;=\; \nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t) + w\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p(c \mid x_t) \;=\; \nabla_{x_t} \log \big[p(x_t \mid c)^w \, p(x_t)^{1-w}\big],$$ that is, sampling from the *reweighted* law $p_w \propto p(x_t\|c)^w p(x_t)^{1-w}$ — exactly the family of theorem 5.1 (RLHF) with $w \leftrightarrow 1/\beta$.

::: proof
Linearity of the score: $\hat\epsilon_w = (1 - w)\hat\epsilon_u + w \hat\epsilon_c$ (rewrite the combination); each term is proportional to the gradient of the corresponding log-density, so the sum is the gradient of the *sum* of the logs. For the conditional term, Bayes' rule $p(x_t \mid c) \propto p(c \mid x_t)\, p(x_t)$ gives $\nabla \log p(x_t\|c)^w p(x_t)^{1-w} = w\nabla\log p(c\|x_t) + \nabla \log p(x_t)$ — which is precisely the formula of *classifier guidance* with weight $w$: CFG obtains it *without a classifier*, by training the same network with conditioning dropout. At $w = 1$: pure conditional model; $w > 1$: over-guidance (fidelity $\uparrow$, diversity $\downarrow$, color saturation — the classic visual symptom); $w < 1$: interpolation toward the unconditional. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 7.2. ControlNet: spatial control, without breaking the pre-training

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.2 — ControlNet architecture (Zhang, Rao & Agrawala, ICCV 2023)]{.tag} Let $F(x ; \Theta)$ be a frozen UNet block (operation on the activation $x$ of layer $i$). ControlNet branches off a *trainable copy* initialized at $\Theta$ and locks the output with two *null* convolutions (zero-convolutions): $$y \;=\; F(x;\Theta) \;+\; Z_2\Big(F_c\big(Z_1(c;\Theta_{z_1});\ \Theta_c\big);\ \Theta_{z_2}\Big),$$ where $c$ is the control map (Canny edges, depth, skeletal pose…); $Z_i$ is a $1\times1$ convolution with *zero weights at initialization*.

::: proof
**Identity property at the start.** At $t = 0$: $Z_2(\cdot) = W_2 \, h = 0$ since $W_2 = 0$ — the branch outputs exactly zero, and the composed model is *identically* the pre-trained model: fine-tuning starts from the initial quality, without "catastrophic shift". **The gradient does not vanish.** The derivative of the output with respect to $W_2$ equals $\partial y / \partial W_2 = h_c \neq 0$ (the copy $F_c$, initialized at $\Theta$, produces nonzero activations): the first update pulls $W_2$ away from zero, which then *unlocks* the gradients toward $F_c$ and $Z_1$ (which were zero as long as $W_2 = 0$, by the chain rule). Compare the naive alternative (branching $F_c$ directly): at step 0, uncontrolled random noise is added to the activations of the frozen UNet and destroys the coherence of the output for hundreds of steps. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Why a "copy" and not a "new network"]{.tag} The copy inherits the pre-trained features: control learns *the correspondence control map → existing rich features*, not vision from scratch — hence the data efficiency (a few thousand pairs suffice for a new type of control). This is a general pattern of the module: condition around a frozen model and protect the interface with an identity initialization (the mask of ch. 3 is the exact analogue for discrete slots: allow only what preserves the invariant).
:::

### 7.3. Editing a real image: inversion and null-text

::: prop
[Proposition 7.3 — DDIM inversion and its failure under CFG]{.tag} DDIM defines a deterministic step linking $x_t$ and $x_{t-1}$ via the prediction $\hat x_0(x_t, c)$; *inversion* traverses the relation backwards (reminder: Multimodal GenAI module ch. 4): $$x_{t+1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t+1}}\, \hat x_0(x_t, c) + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{t+1}}\; \hat\epsilon_c(x_t, c).$$ With CFG, the applied "noise" depends on a $w$-combination of the conditional/unconditional predictions; inversion becomes an implicit equation (the step depends on $x_t$ through two networks): error accumulates, the reconstruction drifts. **Null-text inversion** (Mokady et al., CVPR 2023): keep the inversion trajectory as an *anchor* and optimize, step by step, the *null* condition embedding $c_\varnothing^{(t)}$ to minimize $\|\hat x_0\big(x_t; c, c_\varnothing^{(t)}\big) - x_0\|^2$ — a few dozen gradient steps per image; editing (Prompt-to-Prompt: substituting the cross-attention maps; InstructPix2Pix: learning editing on synthetic data) then operates *along* this faithful trajectory.
:::

::: ex
[Example 7.4 — CFG by hand (pen-and-paper, in the graph module's format)]{.tag} Vocabulary of 3 artistic "directions", logits of step $t$ without conditioning: $(\text{painting}: 2.0,\ \text{photo}: 1.5,\ \text{3D}: 0.5)$; with condition "watercolor": $(3.0,\ 0.5,\ 0.5)$. At $w = 3$: guided logits $= (1-w)\,u + w\,c = (-4.0,\ -1.0,\ 0.5)$… in the equivalent additive form $u + w(c - u) = (5.0,\ -1.0,\ 0.5)$ — softmax $\approx (0.95, 0.007,\ 0.04)$: the target style crushes the distribution, exactly like the molecular CFG of example 7.3 of the Graph Generative Models module. $w = 8$ → a single mode survives: the curve of ch. 9, readable on a single step.
:::

## 8. Controlling graph generators {#ch8}

Synthesis chapter: the Graph Generative Models module (M2) develops each family in detail — here we reread its chapters 3, 4, and 5 through the grid of ch. 2, to show that the theory of control there is *identical* to that of text and images.

::: thm
[Theorem 8.1 — Three controls, three mechanisms, one grid]{.tag}

1.  **Hard constraints: chemical valence**. Each decoding step masks the bonds that would exceed the remaining valence $r_v$ of atom $v$ — NeVAE (AAAI 2019) pushes validity above 90% without post-processing (versus a few percent otherwise); GraphAF masks likewise and reaches 100% with rules (68% without). This is *word for word* theorem 2.2: renormalization over the legal set $\mathcal{L}$, guaranteed by construction;
2.  **Gradient guidance**: GraphAF (ICLR 2020) — each decision starts from a $z_t \sim \mathcal N(0,1)$ passed through a flow; to maximize a property $Q(G)$ (solubility, docking), one moves $z_t$ along $\nabla_{z_t} Q(G_t)$ *during* generation — the guidance strength is the gradient step, the fidelity/diversity trade-off is measured there (the graph module ch. 4 derives it);
3.  **Conditioning + inpainting**: DiGress (ICLR 2023) trains the denoiser with a descriptor $c$ sometimes masked (classifier-free: thm 7.1 transposed) and freezes partial scaffolds; the discrete posterior allows generating *around* an imposed motif — the exact analogue of the image null-text/inpainting of ch. 7.
:::

  Control               Mechanism (ch. 2)           Where (graph module)    Text analogue        Image analogue
  --------------------- --------------------------- ----------------------- -------------------- --------------------
  Chemical validity     mask (renormalization)      ch. 3 (NeVAE)           automaton of ch. 3   —
  Target property $Q$   gradient guidance           ch. 4 (GraphAF)         steering (ch. 4)     CFG (ch. 7)
  Imposed scaffold      conditioning + inpainting   ch. 5 (DiGress)         forced prefix        null-text (ch. 7)
  Text → graph          heavy conditioning (LLM)    ch. 7 (text-to-graph)   prompting            full text-to-image

::: note
[What graphs teach control]{.tag} Two specific lessons. (i) *Local* constraints (valence) are trivially masked, *global* constraints (connectivity, ring size) are not: the corresponding automaton would be exponential — the search for "tractable global constraints" is open; (ii) the evaluation of control is the most mature there (validity/uniqueness/novelty + FCD; graph module ch. 6) — it is the template of ch. 9.
:::

## 9. Evaluating control: fidelity versus diversity {#ch9}

Controlling without measuring is believing. This chapter sets the protocol: two axes (fidelity, diversity), one curve (the strength sweep), one decomposition (precision/recall), and a bound showing that the trade-off is *structural*, not an engineering defect.

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — Fidelity and diversity]{.tag} **Control fidelity**: $\mathrm{Fid}(S) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \mathbf{1}[y_i \in S]$ (pass rate; or a continuous metric — property score, similarity to the prompt). **Diversity**: mean intra-batch distance $\mathrm{Div} = \frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j} d(y_i, y_j)$ (self-BLEU for text, LPIPS distance for images, Tanimoto for molecules — graph module ch. 6); or entropy of the effective law. **Quality** in the data-fidelity sense: FID (recall of the Multimodal GenAI module ch. 8), perplexity under a reference model.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 9.2 — The trade-off is structural (entropy bound)]{.tag} Let $S \subset \mathcal{Y}^\*$ be the admissible set ($\|S\| = m$ finite; for sequences, consider outputs of length $\leq L$ over a vocabulary of size $k$: $m \leq k^L$, the whole space). Every law $\tilde p$ supported on $S$ satisfies $$H(\tilde p) \;\leq\; \log m \;=\; H_{\max}(\mathcal{Y}^{\leq L}) \;-\; \log\frac{k^L}{m}.$$

::: proof
Entropy is maximal for the uniform law (Gibbs' inequality: for every $p$ on $S$, $\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, \mathrm{Unif}_S) = \log m - H(p) \geq 0$, with equality iff uniform). Support constraint → entropy ceiling lowered by $\log(k^L/m)$: every order of magnitude of constraint dividing the number of admissible outputs by $e$ costs 1 nat of maximal diversity. Guidance acts likewise but *smoothly*: $p_w \propto p^{1-w}\mathrm{score}(c)^w$ concentrates mass on the modes compatible with $c$ — the effective entropy decreases monotonically in the usual cases (theorems 5.1 and 7.1: the KL from the start is exactly the price paid); hence the curve. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 9.3 — The control curve (protocol)]{.tag} For each strength $w \in \{0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, \dots\}$ (or the watermark's $\delta$, steering's $\alpha$, RLHF's $\beta^{-1}$): generate a fixed batch (same seeds), measure $(\mathrm{Fid}(w), \mathrm{Div}(w))$, plot the trajectory. Reading: (i) a method *dominates* if its curve is above/to the right of another's everywhere; (ii) the "elbow" (fidelity stops growing, diversity collapses) is the recommended tuning point; (iii) complete with the precision/recall decomposition (Kynkäänniemi et al., NeurIPS 2019): *precision* measures the quality of the occupied modes, *recall* the coverage of the data's modes — over-guidance kills recall (abandoned modes) before precision. Classic anti-protocol: plot only fidelity ("100% valid JSON!") and keep silent that the model now emits only three templates — mode collapse, control version.
:::

::: ex
[Example 9.4 — Toy curve, by hand]{.tag} Law over 4 outputs with probabilities $(0.4,\ 0.3,\ 0.2,\ 0.1)$; exponential control with score $c = (3,\ 3,\ 0,\ 0)$ at strength $w$. At $w=0$: entropy 1.85 nats; $w=1$: $\propto (8.0,\ 6.0,\ 0.2,\ 0.1) \to$ probs $(0.56,\ 0.42,\ 0.014,\ 0.007)$, entropy 0.97; $w=2$: $(7.2,\ 5.4,\ 0.004,\ 0.001)$ — two modes at 99%, entropy 0.69; $w = 4$ collapse onto mode 1. Mean fidelity to the score: 0.5 → 0.98 → 0.99. The pair $(\mathrm{Fid}, H)$ draws exactly the frontier of theorem 9.2. Generalize in exercise 4.
:::

## 10. Attacks on control and robustness {#ch10}

Control is a promise; this chapter tests the promise. Four surfaces, in the module's order: the mask, steering/RLHF, the watermark, spatial control.

::: thm
[Theorem 10.1 — Attacking constrained decoding (hostile content *inside* the format)]{.tag} The mask guarantees $y \in S$ — *syntax*, never *semantics*. An injected prompt can fill a perfectly valid JSON with `{"instruction": "ignore the previous rules"}`; a constrained tool call can be diverted into hostile parameters (prompt injection in agents: cf. Explainability module ch. 5). Second: the *complexity* of the grammar is a surface — an ambiguous grammar explodes the number of states (subset construction $2^{\|Q\|}$) and allows a denial of service *of the control itself*; finally the *tokenizer interaction*: changing the tokenizer invalidates the state→tokens index (recompilation). Defenses: downstream semantic validation (schema + bounds: $\delta$-constraints beyond the regular), state-size limits, server-side pre-compiled grammars (defense-in-depth pattern of the Explainability module ch. 6).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 10.2 — Attacks on the watermark (and impossibility results)]{.tag}

1.  **Edits**: paraphrase, synonym substitution, emoji/homoglyph insertion, LLM rewriting — every exchange of a green token for a red one costs $\approx 1/\sqrt{T\gamma(1-\gamma)}$ in $z$; to bring $\mathbb{E}[z] = 6$ below 2 one must rewrite a substantial fraction of the tokens, at the price of quality;
2.  **Spoofing**: can an attacker *without the key* mark an innocent text to accuse a provider? Public-key schemes and the reliability analysis (Kirchenbauer et al., ICLR 2024 — "On the Reliability"; already referenced in the LLMs module) quantify these false accusations: key management becomes the real problem (revocation, multi-keys, aggregated tests);
3.  **Undetectability**: Sadasivan et al. (2023) show that a good enough paraphraser drives *every* detector toward chance; Christ, Gunn & Zamir (2024) bound what is achievable: robustness is bought only in distortion. Operational conclusion: a watermark is a *provenance marker*, not a cryptographic proof of origin; stacking it (text + audio + image, multi-key styles) is the realistic strategy.
:::

::: note
[Attacks on guidance and steering, in brief]{.tag} Steering (ch. 4) has no support guarantee: a behavior removed on a test prompt reappears out of distribution (jailbreaks by rephrasing, other languages, encodings); RLHF is vulnerable to *reward hacking* (ch. 5) and preference attacks; CFG/ControlNet: *adversarial prompts* (forbidden contents rephrased), *image injections* (diverted inpainting, editing of persons — deepfakes), hence mandatory marking (theorem 1.3) and downstream moderation. A vast program crossing the Explainability (LLM security) and Responsible AI modules.
:::

::: def
[Definition 10.3 — Robustness budget (the quantity to remember)]{.tag} For a fidelity control $c$ and a family of attacks $\mathcal A$, one defines the **degradation** $\Delta(w) = \mathrm{Fid}(w) - \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \mathcal A}[\mathrm{Fid}(w, a)]$. A robust control has flat $\Delta$ in $w$; the evaluation of ch. 9 must therefore be repeated *under attack* — the complete protocol fits in one sentence: *plot the fidelity/diversity curve, with and without an adversary, at fixed quality budget*.
:::

## Exercises / Labs {#ex}

1.  **Lab: constrained decoding on regex (the module's lab).** (a) Build the DFA of `^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{4}$` by hand (states, co-accessible pruning), table $\\mathrm{Adm}(q)$ on a mini-vocabulary including the multi-character tokens `"12/"`, `"19"`; (b) implement `DfaMask` (code of ch. 3) with a small GPT's tokenizer; (c) plug in as a HuggingFace `LogitsProcessor` and generate 1,000 dates; (d) measure the pass rate with/without mask and the time overhead compared to free generation.

    ::: proof
    Guidance (expected results): without constraint, the pass rate of a small model on the exact requested date plateaus (`2026-08-26`, `26/08/2026` formats mixed); with mask: 100% — including *false* but syntactically valid dates (`31/02/2026`): semantics requires one more layer (bounds validation), the conclusion of ch. 10 experienced in the lab. Overhead: \~0% (the mask is negligible next to the transformer pass); the real cost is the *precomputation* of the index, paid once. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
2.  **The z-test in full.** With $\\gamma = 0.5$, $\\delta = 2$: (a) simulate 10,000 human texts (iid uniform tokens) and empirically verify $\\mathbb{P}(z > 4) \\approx 3 \\times 10\^{-5}$; (b) estimate $p\_\\delta$ empirically by simulating the biased softmax at temperature 1; (c) plot the power of the test as a function of $T \\in [20, 500]$; (d) derive the minimal $T$ for power 0.9 (compare with example 6.3); (e) repeat with $\\gamma = 0.25$ and conclude on the tuning.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: (a) the distribution of $z$ sticks to $\\mathcal N(0,1)$ from $T \\geq 50$ (De Moivre-Laplace); (b) $p\_\\delta$ depends on the standard deviation of the logits; with logits $\\mathcal N(0,1)$, $p\_\\delta \\approx 0.75$; (c) sigmoidal power in $\\sqrt{T}$; (d) $T \\approx 30$-50 for $(0.5, 2)$; (e) $\\gamma = 0.25$ divides the variance under H0 ($\\times 0.75$) and concentrates the signal — slightly better at fixed $\\delta$, but lower text quality: the triple trade-off of ch. 6 is *verified numerically*. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
3.  **Steering step by step.** On GPT-2 small: build $v = h\^{(l)}(\\texttt{Love}) - h\^{(l)}(\\texttt{Hate})$ for $l \\in \\{2, 5, 8, 10\\}$; sweep $\\alpha \\in \\{-2, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2\\}$; measure (i) frequency of "marriage" words, (ii) perplexity, (iii) intra-batch diversity (self-BLEU).

    ::: proof
    Guidance: the topic effect is clear and quasi-linear in $\\alpha$ at small $\\alpha$ (prop. 4.3), perplexity moves little up to $\\alpha \\approx 2$ then derails; diversity drops as $\|\\alpha\|$ grows — the same fidelity/diversity curve as CFG (ch. 9), again. Discuss: why does steering "succeed" on broad latent concepts and fail to impose a precise format (answer: full support — ch. 2). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
4.  **Theoretical fidelity/diversity frontier.** Prove the entropy bound 9.2 (Gibbs), then generalize example 9.4: arbitrary initial law, score $c$, plot $(\\mathrm{Fid}(w), H(w))$ for $w \\in [0, 10]$ and verify that the curve converges to the corner $(\\max c, 0)$. What happens to the curve if $c$ is noisy?

    ::: proof
    Guidance: normalize $p_w \\propto p\\, e\^{w c}$ (exponential family); $H(w)$ decreases (derive $dH/dw = -w\\,\\mathrm{Var}\_w(c)$ — a classic identity: the derivative of the log-partition gives the variance, that of the entropy its weighted variance); with noise, a plateau appears before the collapse: the analyst chooses the elbow. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
5.  **Zero-convolution: the gradient under the magnifier.** For the ControlNet branch of theorem 7.2 at initialization: (a) show that the output is exactly zero; (b) compute $\\partial y / \\partial W_2$ and show it is nonzero; (c) show that $\\partial y / \\partial \\Theta_c = 0$ at initialization and explain why this is *not* a deadlock; (d) compare with random initialization (branching $F_c$ without $Z$): simulate 10 descent steps on a toy task and compare the initial losses.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: (a) $Z_2 = W_2 h = 0$; (b) $\\partial y/\\partial W_2 = h_c \\neq 0$ (activations of the copy initialized at $\\Theta$); (c) chain rule through $W_2 = 0$, unlocked as soon as $W_2$'s first update happens; (d) the variant without zero-conv starts from a high loss and destroys the frozen model's output — the experiment reproduces the motivation figure of the ControlNet paper. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
6.  **Attacking your own watermark (bonus).** After lab 2: paraphrase the marked texts (via an LLM, instruction "rewrite with the same ideas"), measure the drop in $z$ as a function of the rate of replaced tokens, and estimate the rate needed to fall below $z = 2$. Conclude on the sentence "a watermark is a marker, not a proof".

    ::: proof
    Guidance: each green→red replacement shifts $\\mathbb E[z]$ by about $(p\_\\delta - \\gamma)\\big/\\sqrt{T\\gamma(1-\\gamma)}$; going from $\\mathbb E[z] = 7$ to 2 requires rewriting the majority of tokens — the text that survives the attack is so transformed that *content* traceability (plagiarism) becomes the issue again, not that of *the machine*. Loop closed with ch. 10. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
